stock: 235/75R15 on 15x6 steel wheels (1996 NL GLX, Australia, per owner)
15-inch alloys on US Montero LS and SR (Bring a Trailer listings)

max_tire.note: An Australian owner calls 31x10.5R15 'a good tyre size' for the NL. BaT's 1994 Montero SR runs 31x10.50R15s on factory 15-inch alloys, and a 1995 Pajero sold on 265/70R16. Expect some contact at full lock and full stuff; bigger tyres need a lift.

items.title: NADI driver airbag inflator
items.summary: Non-azide driver inflators can absorb moisture and rupture or under-inflate. In Australia, Mitsubishi offers to buy back affected NL Pajeros because no replacement inflator exists.

items.title: Crankshaft pulley bolt can loosen (3.0)
items.summary: On 3.0-litre Monteros the crank-pulley bolt can loosen and the pulley can fall off.

items.title: Front wheel-side brake hoses can crack
items.summary: At full lock and full suspension travel the front hoses can crack and leak fluid. 96V143002 covers Caribbean-market trucks.

items.title: Front lower brake hoses can crack
items.summary: The front lower brake hoses can develop a crack, causing loss of brake fluid.

items.title: Front brake lines chafe through
items.summary: Front brake lines can develop pinholes from chafing on the edge of the inner-fender pass-through hole.

items.title: Accessory cargo mat stops third-row seats latching
items.summary: Accessory cargo mats in the third-row and cargo area can interfere with the folding third seats' latches.

items.title: Airbag warning labels too small
items.summary: The bilingual removable airbag warning labels didn't meet FMVSS 208 size requirements (Caribbean-market trucks).

items.title: Aftermarket Reese trailer hitch weld (equipment)
items.summary: The receiver weld on a Reese hitch can break. This is an equipment recall, not a Mitsubishi campaign.

tsbs.title: Pitman-arm ball-joint inspection (Japan service notice)
tsbs.ref: Mitsubishi Japan notice (all V20 codes incl. V55W)
tsbs.summary: Inspection procedure for old, hard-used trucks with integral ball-nut steering: check the stud for wear, use moly chassis grease, torque relay-rod nuts to 44 N·m, and replace boots every 5 years.

timeline.change: Second generation launched in Japan on 22 January 1991. Super Select 4WD, multi-mode ABS and optional electronic dampers. 6G72 3.0 SOHC 12v V6 and 4D56 2.5 intercooled turbo-diesel. Exports began later in the year
First US model year for the second-generation Montero (Active-Trac 4WD)
July: 6G74 3.5 DOHC 24v V6 (US SR: 215 hp) and 4M40 2.8 intercooled turbo-diesel arrive, with a larger transmission and transfer case. Slight restyle
3.0 V6 gains a 24-valve head and coil-pack ignition (US: 177 hp / 188 lb-ft). 2.4 four added for some SWB markets
May: Japanese 'Wide' models with wheel-arch flares and a 3.5 GDI V6. Australia's NL switches to a SOHC 3.5 (US 1998: 200 hp). Pajero Evolution (V55W) goes on sale in September/October

Export and Gulf trucks get the 'blister' wide-fender facelift; airbags standard on 3.5 models in those markets. Beware the NADI driver airbag: 1998–2000 US Monteros are under recall 20V035000 for a new inflator, and in Australia Mitsubishi is buying back NL Pajeros built 31 May 1996 to 30 September 2000 because no replacement exists
The monocoque third-generation Pajero replaces it in Japan (August)
Final US model year for the second-generation Montero; the third generation arrives as a 2001 model

identify.intro: Many second-generation Pajeros in the US are Japanese imports, and Evolutions get faked. The chassis code and build plate tell you what you're looking at.

items.head: Chassis codes
items.body: Mitsubishi's own notice lists the second-generation codes: V14V, V21W, V23C, V23W, V24C, V24V, V24W, V25C, V25W, V26C, V26W, V34V, V43W, V44W, V45W, V46V, V46W and V55W. JDMBUYSELL advises confirming the complete code on the frame or VIN plate.

items.head: A real Evolution
items.body: Check the plate for E-V55W, a 3,496 cc 6G74 MIVEC V6 rated at 280 PS, a three-door body and independent multi-link/double-wishbone rear suspension. Overfenders, twin rear fins and a bonnet scoop are easy to copy; the rear suspension isn't.

items.head: DOHC or SOHC 3.5
items.body: Australian owners say NJ and NK trucks used the DOHC 3.5 and the NL a SOHC 3.5. In the US, the 1994 SR is rated at 215 hp (DOHC) and a 1998 Montero at 200 hp.

items.head: Locker and Super Select
items.body: A factory rear locker shows up as a dash switch and air lines to the rear diff, and works only in 4HLc or 4LLc. Every second-generation truck has the Super Select gated lever; US trucks are badged Active-Trac.

items.head: Grey-import tells
items.body: Australian owners say mirrors on the front mudguards and higher-spec interiors mark a Japanese import. In the US, right-hand drive and a km/h speedometer give it away.

capability.note: Owner-reported; towing pushes the 3.5 to about 20 L/100 km
V55W manual, per Motor-Fan catalogue via JDMBUYSELL

values.intro: Ordinary second-generation Pajeros and Monteros are still cheap. The Evolution is the collector's car, and it's climbing.

ranges.cond: Project / tired US Montero or import

values.note: Based on Bring a Trailer sold results. Second-generation Pajeros and Monteros sold from 2020 to October 2026 ran from $3,500 (a 1992 turbo-diesel) to $19,500 (a 1998 Exceed GLS turbo-diesel manual), with an 18k-mile 1998 Montero at $16,000; most went for $7,500–13,500. Eighteen sold Evolutions from October 2024 to October 2026 ranged from $19,500 to $49,997.

paragraphs: NHTSA's import exemption covers vehicles at least 25 years old, counted from each vehicle's own manufacture date (49 CFR 591.5(i)). As of October 2026 that includes every first- and second-generation Pajero, so right-hand-drive Japanese-market trucks, the 2.5 and 2.8 turbo-diesels and the Pajero Evolution can all be imported. Bring a Trailer has sold dozens of them since 2016.

The EPA exemption is separate. It requires the vehicle to be at least 21 years old and in its original configuration, or fitted with an equivalent or newer EPA-certified engine and emissions system, so keep the import paperwork. State titling and emissions rules vary, and California is the hardest. Canada's threshold is 15 years, which doesn't make a truck legal to bring into the US.
